cf.title: Make the logical replication conflict messages more like each other

input.subject: Make the logical replication conflict messages more like each other

verdict_reasoning: Nothing that survived stops the proposal at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is a fixable wording point: two proposed reason lines are less exact than the detail lines they introduce. The proposal only rewords DETAIL text in errdetail_apply_conflict and adds no new interface. Confidence is low because no patch exists and the thread has one supporting reply.

brief.title: Reword logical replication conflict detail messages to share one pattern
brief.problem: The errdetail messages for logical replication apply conflicts, built in errdetail_apply_conflict in conflict.c, use mixed wording and structure. Only some conflict types give a general reason line before the detail line, and some lack a final period. The thread names log readers in general and does not cite a specific user complaint.
brief.proposed_design: Every conflict type gets a first line with the general reason ("The row to update was not found") and then a detail line starting with "It was ..." for the origin and transaction. Every message ends with a period, and the wording follows the logical replication conflicts page of the docs. The unique-key detail lines stay the same.
user_visible_surface: Changed DETAIL text of apply-worker conflict log messages for all conflict types, such as update_origin_differs, update_deleted and delete_missing.
Unique-key conflicts get a new first line, "The row to insert violates a constraint", which replaces "Could not apply remote change".
author_claims: Consistent wording makes these closely related messages easier to read.
The new wording is closer to the conflict descriptions in the documentation.
A supporter says consistency helps users match on wording in logs and helps future conflict types follow one style.
brief.thread_state: The author got no replies for about two months and opened CommitFest entry 7043; Ajin Cherian later gave a +1 to the general idea. The author says he will not write a patch until there is agreement, and no patch is visible.
unclear: No patch exists, so reviewers cannot see the final strings or the regression and TAP test output changes.
The proposal does not discuss tools or scripts that parse the current DETAIL text, which the reworded messages would break.
The proposal does not say whether the docs page needs changes to match the new text.
The proposal does not say why the general reason line uses "violates a constraint" when the detail names only unique indexes.

objections.title: New reason lines can contradict the detail lines they introduce
objections.failure_scenario: An apply worker hits insert_exists on a plain unique index that has no constraint and logs "The row to insert violates a constraint". The DBA looks in pg_constraint, finds no matching entry, and loses time before reading the next line about the unique index. In update_origin_differs, the log says "modified by another origin" and then "It was modified locally".
objections.argument: Message #1 adds summary lines that are less exact than the detail lines below them. The insert_exists and update_exists checks look only at unique indexes, and elsewhere Postgres names the object exactly, as in "violates unique constraint". Calling a local change "another origin" is defensible only from the remote side, and the message does not say so. The proposal is about consistency, so a committer would likely ask that the summary lines first agree with the detail lines they introduce.
objections.author_must_show: Can the reason lines say exactly what was detected, such as a unique index and a local or other-origin change, without contradicting the detail line?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 pairs "modified by another origin" with "It was modified locally", and "violates a constraint" with detail lines that name only unique indexes. The pg_constraint half is weaker, because Postgres already reports plain unique index violations as "violates unique constraint", but the wording concern stands as fixable.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The reworded messages come from the logical replication apply worker; replication behaviour does not change.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Changed message text needs new translations, so the change fits a new major version only.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: One-time translator and expected-output updates; later conflict types must follow the shared pattern.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Can the reason line for insert_exists and update_exists name a unique index or unique key instead of "a constraint"?
How should the update_origin_differs and delete_origin_differs reason line read when the detail line says "It was modified locally"?
Does the logical replication conflicts page of the docs need changes to match the new text?
Which regression and TAP test expected outputs change, and by how much?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the logical replication apply worker and conflict detection code, and the error message style guide. No committer has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The final wording of about a dozen DETAIL strings, their translations and the changed test output. The liability is small and ends once the strings settle.
committability.author_follow_up: The author pinged the thread twice and opened the CommitFest entry, and says in message #1 that he will write the patch once there is agreement.

priority.reason: The change rewords strings in one function and benefits people who read apply-worker conflict logs. It is waiting for agreement from someone who knows the area, because the author will not write a patch without it and only one +1 has arrived.

provisional_note: No patch exists, so the final strings, the translation impact and the test output changes could not be judged. The verdict rests on the strings suggested in message #1.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Detection and resolution of logical replication conflict
precedents_retrieved.authors: Zhijie Hou (houzj), shveta malik (shvetam), Nisha Moond (nishamoond)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal adds conflict detection and resolution to the logical replication apply worker, with conflict types such as insert_exists, update_origin_differs, update_missing and delete_missing. Users pick a built-in resolver (for example apply_remote, keep_local, skip, error or last_update_wins) per conflict type, first as a global setting and later as a CONFLICT RESOLVER clause on CREATE SUBSCRIPTION.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The patch set was still under review at v17 in October 2024, and the last message shown, from 2024-10-28, has no reply. Two items were still open at that point: clock-skew handling, and a race in which DirtySnapshot index scans miss rows and report update_missing or delete_missing instead of the origin_differs conflicts.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow self-conflicting INSERT INTO .. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATEs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE accept a command whose own proposed rows conflict with each other, as DO NOTHING already does. Today such a command fails with "command cannot affect row a second time".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Peter Geoghegan voted against it, and the CFM returned it citing those two votes. Andres Freund objected that the patch makes one command update a row it inserted, producing cmin == cmax and breaking heap visibility rules. The author then found visibility bugs in his own patch. Peter Geoghegan argued that updating the same row twice in one command is not desirable and asked who would want it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To me it seems as if allowing the same command to update the same row more than once is just not desirable in general.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add errdetail() with PID and UID about source of termination signal
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch installs signal handlers with SA_SIGINFO, records the sender PID and UID when a backend gets SIGTERM, and adds them to the termination message as "Signal sent by PID %d, UID %d." It has no GUC and works only where SA_SIGINFO exists, such as Linux and FreeBSD.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Reviewers supported the idea and asked only for style and code fixes, and the author posted v5 in response. No later message gives a reason for the withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: conflict handling for COPY FROM
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Andrew Dunstan, Alvaro Herrera
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets COPY FROM skip rows that fail with unique or exclusion constraint violations, and later some format errors, up to an error limit set by a GUC or option. Failed rows go to a log file named in the command so the user can examine them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that writing a server-side log file requires superuser rights, unlike COPY from STDIN. Andrew Dunstan and Andres suggested logging failed rows to a table or returning them as rows instead. Andres marked the entry returned with feedback after the author did not answer these comments for weeks. The author's later version reported skipped rows as warnings, which Alvaro Herrera called useless for this purpose; he supported returning rows.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Again, that requires super user permissions (in contrast to copy from/to stdin/out).

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert dubious message wording change.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert dubious message wording change.

precedents_retrieved.title: conflict handling for COPY FROM
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an error-limit option to COPY FROM (first ON CONFLICT IGNORE, later ERROR_LIMIT, with -1 for no limit) that skips rows failing unique or exclusion constraints, using the speculative insertion infrastructure, and also skips some row-format errors. Malformed rows are reported as warnings, and constraint-violating rows are sent back to the client as tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane reviewed the version marked ready for committer and judged it not committable. The option covers only errors raised in COPY itself, not bad numbers or bad encoding. Sending rejected rows back to the client breaks the wire protocol and can deadlock, and the warnings print whole input lines against the message style guidelines. He saw such features in COPY as a dead end and suggested staging tables plus new INSERT ... ON CONFLICT actions; David Steele returned the patch based on that review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: On the whole, I feel like adding this sort of functionality to COPY itself is a dead end.

precedents_retrieved.title: DOCS: Make the Server Application docs synopses more consistent
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set makes the synopses of the Server Application reference pages consistent: it uses 'datadir' for the --pgdata argument, puts [option...] first, fixes markup and typos in pg_waldump and pg_walsummary, and adds an Options section to pg_controldata. It also adds synopsis guidelines to the documentation style guide.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. David G. Johnston supported the direction and discussed details such as short versus long options and whether env-var-backed options should appear optional. The last message is the v3 split patch set from April 2025, with no reply before the entry was withdrawn in March 2026.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow using replication origins in SQL level parallel sessions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a variant pg_replication_origin_session_setup(text, int) so that several SQL sessions can use the same replication origin at once. Logical replication parallel apply workers already share an origin this way, and the patch exposes that to external replication systems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila pointed out that another thread already discusses the same feature and asked the author to give input there. The entry was then withdrawn, so the work appears to have continued in that other thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We are already discussing the same feature in an email thread [1]. Can
you check that and share your inputs there?

precedents_retrieved.title: Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Track invalidation_reason in pg_replication_slots.
Reverted commit(s): Track conflict_reason in pg_replication_slots.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Till now, the reason for replication slot invalidation is not tracked
directly in pg_replication_slots. A recent commit 007693f2a3 added
'conflict_reason' to show the reasons for slot conflict/invalidation, but
only for logical slots.

This commit adds a new column 'invalidation_reason' to show invalidation
reasons for both physical and logical slots. And, this commit also turns
'conflict_reason' text column to 'conflicting' boolean column (effectively
reverting commit 007693f2a3). The 'conflicting' column is true for
invalidation reasons 'rows_removed' and 'wal_level_insufficient' because
those make the slot conflict with recovery. When 'conflicting' is true,
one can now look at the new 'invalidation_reason' column for the reason
for the logical slot's conflict with recovery.

The new 'invalidation_reason' column will also be useful to track other
invalidation reasons in the future commit.

precedents_retrieved.title: transaction statistics of logical replication subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed counting failed transactions and their sizes in pg_stat_replication_slots, so that users could tell successful logical decoding from repeated failed attempts. By the last version, the patch instead added apply_commit_count and apply_rollback_count columns to pg_stat_subscription_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila noted that pg_stat_database already shows committed and rolled-back transactions per database, so the new counters largely duplicate it, and he asked whether anyone saw value in them. Masahiko Sawada agreed that commit and rollback counts without transaction sizes no longer meet the original goal and have no concrete use case. The author then marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I’m concerned that adding only apply_commit_count
and apply_rollback_count ends up adding the duplicate statistics with
no concrete use cases.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert logical snapshot filename format change in SnapBuildSnapshotExists().
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert logical snapshot filename format change in SnapBuildSnapshotExists().
Reverted commit(s): Standardize LSN formatting by zero padding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 2633dae2e48 standardized LSN formatting but mistakenly changed
the logical snapshot filename format in SnapBuildSnapshotExists() from
"%X-%X.snap" to "%08X-%08X.snap". Other code still used the original
"%X-%X.snap" format, causing the replication slot synchronization worker
to fail to find existing snapshot files and produce excessive log messages.

This commit restores the original "%X-%X.snap" format
in SnapBuildSnapshotExists() to resolve the issue.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert refactoring of hex code to src/common/
Reverted commit(s): move hex_decode() to /common so it can be called from frontend; Rework refactoring of hex and encoding routines; Remove PG_SHA*_DIGEST_STRING_LENGTH from sha2.h
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This is a combined revert of the following commits:
- c3826f8, a refactoring piece that moved the hex decoding code to
src/common/.  This code was cleaned up by aef8948, as it originally
included no overflow checks in the same way as the base64 routines in
src/common/ used by SCRAM, making it unsafe for its purpose.
- aef8948, a more advanced refactoring of the hex encoding/decoding code
to src/common/ that added sanity checks on the result buffer for hex
decoding and encoding.  As reported by Hans Buschmann, those overflow
checks are expensive, and it is possible to see a performance drop in
the decoding/encoding of bytea or LOs the longer they are.  Simple SQLs
working on large bytea values show a clear difference in perf profile.
- ccf4e27, a cleanup made possible by aef8948.

The reverts of all those commits bring back the performance of hex
decoding and encoding back to what it was in ~13.  Fow now and
post-beta3, this is the simplest option.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the precedent list has no matching row. Message #1 says the author first raised this idea in another thread, where it was ruled out of scope. Being out of scope there is not a rejection on the merits, so no earlier rejection reason applies here.

Breaking log parsers is not raised as an objection. Postgres does not promise stable message text across major versions, translations already vary it, and the stable conflict=<type> tag in the main message is unchanged.

The proposal only rewords errdetail text in errdetail_apply_conflict, which the apply worker writes to the server log. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol message, replication slot or extension-facing struct, so this angle has nothing to object to. Mixed-version publisher and subscriber pairs see no change in behaviour.

The proposal only rewords the DETAIL text of existing apply-worker conflict messages and adds no new data to them. The origin names, transaction ids, timestamps and key values stay in the same messages, which reach the same server log, so nobody can see or do anything new and there is no privilege or exposure aspect.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to object to. The change rewords existing DETAIL strings for one function in conflict.c. It adds no GUC, catalog, API, hot-path work or external dependency, so a single shared pattern should make later conflict types cheaper to add. The one-time cost is translator updates and expected-output changes in tests, which is normal for any message cleanup. Postgres does not treat message text as a stable interface, so breaking log parsers is not a fit objection. Without a patch I could not check the final strings or the test churn.

No existing feature, extension or tool rewrites these DETAIL strings, so this angle finds nothing already meeting the need. The proposal changes existing messages and adds no second mechanism or anything an extension could provide.

Demand evidence is thin: no user complaint, and one +1 in message #4. Even so, a demand objection would not hold up. Making message wording follow the project's error message style is routine upkeep and does not need field reports. The cost falls on translators and on tools that parse DETAIL text, and tools can match on the conflict type in the main message instead. These messages are recent, so changing them now costs less than changing them later. Without a patch, I could not check the final strings or how many translations they touch.
